  <h1 class="bq-hero-h1 bq-bench-h1">bunqueue vs BullMQ, <em>measured.</em></h1>
  <p class="bq-hero-sub">bunqueue 2.9.20 against BullMQ 6.4.2 on Redis 8.10.2, on one machine with pinned cores, 5 measured runs per number and an exact-delivery check on every run. Where each one is faster, and by how much.</p>
</div>

Measured October 25, 2026. Every table cell is the median of 5 runs after one warm-up run, with the range of the 5 runs in parentheses. BullMQ runs on both Node.js and Bun, and each ratio compares bunqueue with the faster of the two. Pickup-latency and delayed-job rows use bunqueue with `pollTimeout: 5000`, the long-poll mode BullMQ workers use by default; every other bunqueue row uses its defaults.

## Machine and versions

| | |
| --- | --- |
| CPU | AMD Ryzen 9 7950X3D, 16 cores / 32 threads, up to 5.76 GHz, 128 MiB L3 (two CCDs) |
| Memory | 124 GiB |
| Disk | 3x Samsung PM9A3 NVMe (MZQL21T9HCJR) in RAID 5, ext4 |
| System | Debian GNU/Linux 13 (trixie), Linux 6.12.48+deb13-amd64, bare metal, CPU governor performance |
| Pinning | broker on CPUs 2,3,18,19 (two physical cores), clients on 8-15,24-31 (the other CCD) |
| Conditions | a shared server: other services ran during the run, so each cell reports the median of five runs with its range |
| bunqueue | 2.9.20 (npm), server started with `bunqueue start`, clients from `bunqueue/client` on Bun 1.4.4 |
| BullMQ | 6.4.2 with ioredis 6.0.0, on Node.js 24.22.1 and on Bun 1.4.4 |
| Redis | 8.10.2, official Docker image, host networking |

## How it was measured

- One broker at a time, Redis or the bunqueue server, pinned to the same two physical cores. Producers and workers run in separate processes on the other core complex, so the broker never shares a core or a cache with its clients.
- Both libraries use their documented defaults, plus `removeOnComplete` and `removeOnFail` on every job. The bunqueue server runs with `RATE_LIMIT_WINDOW_MS=0`: its per-connection request limit protects a shared server and Redis has no equivalent.
- Every run uses a fresh client process and a new queue. Every consuming run checks that each accepted job was processed exactly once (three times in the retry scenario); a run that loses or duplicates a job fails instead of reporting a number.
- Pickup latency comes from an open-loop producer at a fixed rate and is measured from each job's *scheduled* send time, so a broker that falls behind shows up as latency rather than as a lower offered load.
- In memory: bunqueue's in-memory engine against Redis without persistence. Durable: bunqueue on SQLite (WAL) against Redis with AOF and `appendfsync everysec`, both on the same disk.

| Retries (fail twice, succeed on the third attempt) (jobs/s) | 809 <small>(806–819)</small> | 4,074 <small>(4,047–4,141)</small> | 4,985 <small>(4,978–4,989)</small> | **BullMQ 6.16x** |

On SQLite, bunqueue processes about 4,946 jobs/s with one worker process. At 5,000 and 10,000 jobs/s the offered load is above that, so the backlog grows for the whole 15-second run and the pickup-latency rows measure how far behind the queue fell, not a steady-state latency.

The disk matters for this mode. This server's disk is a RAID 5 array of three NVMe drives. In a diagnostic single run on the same server (one worker process, 50,000 jobs), the one-process drain reached 6,165 jobs/s with the SQLite file on that disk and 11,332 jobs/s with it in RAM (`/dev/shm`): the disk explains about half of the gap, and Redis with AOF `everysec` stays ahead even then. Redis appends to its log and syncs once a second; bunqueue's SQLite engine writes each completed job, with `synchronous = NORMAL` in WAL mode.

## Reproduce it

The harness, its pinned versions and the raw results of this run are in [`bench/vs-bullmq`](https://github.com/egeominotti/bunqueue/tree/main/bench/vs-bullmq) in the repository:

```bash
cd bench/vs-bullmq
bun install --frozen-lockfile
bun src/run.ts
```

It needs Linux, Docker, Bun, Node.js and `taskset`, and takes about 70 minutes. Results land in `results/<timestamp>/`: every run, the medians, and the hardware, kernel and package versions. The [comparison guide](/guide/comparison/) covers features and when BullMQ is the better choice.
